name: Old Arrow Maker
title: Old Arrow Maker
description: A masterwork neoclassical marble sculpture modeled in 1866 by renowned African-American and Native American sculptor Edmonia Lewis. extended_knowledge.inventor_and_date: Invented by American physicist Charles Grafton Page around 1837 and refined in this 1868 patent model. Page was a pioneer in electromagnetism, acoustics, and early electric locomotives.
extended_knowledge.scientific_breakthrough: Page discovered that interrupting a low-voltage primary circuit with a rapid contact breaker (Page's sparker) induced monumental high-voltage surges in a fine secondary wire winding.
extended_knowledge.predecessor_to_modern_tech: The direct technological ancestor of the Ruhmkorff induction coil, automotive ignition coils, fluorescent light ballasts, and modern step-up electrical power grid transformers.
extended_knowledge.construction: Features hand-wound copper coils insulated with silk, brass binding posts, an iron wire core, and an automated mechanical magnetic circuit breaker.

readme_text:
ART006 - Apollo 11 Command Module "Columbia"

Artifact Information

- **Artifact ID:** ART006
- **Artifact Name:** Apollo 11 Command Module "Columbia"
- **Alternate Name:** Apollo 11 Command Module Columbia
- **Type:** SPACECRAFT
- **Domain:** Space & Aerospace History
- **Subdomain:** Human Spaceflight
- **Key Accomplishment:** First Lunar Landing Mission
- **Manufacturer:** North American Rockwell
- **Country of Origin:** United States of America
- **Inventory Number:** A19700102000

---

Description

The Apollo 11 Command Module, "Columbia," served as the living quarters
for the three-person crew during most of the first crewed lunar landing
mission in July 1969.

On July 16, 1969, Neil Armstrong, Edwin "Buzz" Aldrin, and Michael
Collins were launched from Cape Kennedy aboard a Saturn V rocket.

The Command Module was one of three major parts of the Apollo spacecraft.
The other two parts were:

- Service Module
- Lunar Module "Eagle"

The Service Module contained the main spacecraft propulsion system and
consumables.

The Lunar Module "Eagle" was the two-person spacecraft used by Neil
Armstrong and Edwin "Buzz" Aldrin to descend to the Moon's surface on
July 20, 1969.

The Command Module was the only portion of the Apollo spacecraft that
returned to Earth.

---

Historical Significance

Apollo 11 "Columbia" is one of the most significant artifacts in the
history of human spaceflight.

It was used during the first crewed lunar landing mission in July 1969
and carried Neil Armstrong, Edwin "Buzz" Aldrin, and Michael Collins to
the Moon and back.

The Apollo Command Module represents a major milestone in human
spaceflight and the technological development required to conduct
crewed lunar missions.

The Apollo CM Columbia has been designated a:

**"Milestone of Flight"**

by the National Air and Space Museum.

---

Apollo 11 Crew

The Command Module carried three astronauts:

- **Neil A. Armstrong**
- **Edwin "Buzz" Aldrin**
- **Michael Collins**

The crew launched on July 16, 1969.

Armstrong and Aldrin used the Lunar Module "Eagle" to descend to the
Moon's surface on July 20, 1969, while Columbia remained in lunar orbit
with Michael Collins.

---

Apollo Spacecraft Components

The complete Apollo spacecraft consisted of three major components:

```text
Apollo Spacecraft
│
├── Command Module "Columbia"
│   └── Crew living quarters
│
├── Service Module
│   └── Propulsion and consumables
│
└── Lunar Module "Eagle"
    └── Lunar landing vehicle

extended_knowledge.mission_and_crew: Carried Neil Armstrong (Commander), Edwin 'Buzz' Aldrin (Lunar Module Pilot), and Michael Collins (Command Module Pilot) during the historic July 16–24, 1969 lunar landing.
extended_knowledge.reentry_and_heat_shield: Only module of the 363-foot Saturn V rocket stack to return intact. Endured atmospheric reentry at 24,700 mph (Mach 32) and temperatures exceeding 5,000°F (2,760°C) using an ablative phenolic epoxy resin honeycomb heat shield.
extended_knowledge.splashdown_and_recovery: Splashed down in the North Pacific Ocean on July 24, 1969, 812 nautical miles southwest of Hawaii, recovered by the USS Hornet (CV-12).
extended_knowledge.specifications: Base diameter: 3.91 m (12.8 ft), height: 3.48 m (11.4 ft), launch mass: 5,557 kg (12,251 lb). Designated a Smithsonian 'Milestone of Flight'.

---

Description

Discovery was the third Space Shuttle orbiter vehicle to fly in space.
It entered service in 1984 and became the oldest and most utilized
orbiter in the Space Shuttle fleet.

Discovery flew 39 Earth-orbital missions and spent a total of 365 days
in space. During its operational history, it traveled almost 240 million
kilometers (150 million miles), more than any other Space Shuttle
orbiter.

The orbiter carried 184 men and women into space and back, with some
crew members flying more than once. The total number of crew assignments
was 251.

Because Discovery performed every type of mission that the Space Shuttle
was intended to perform, it represents approximately 30 years of U.S.
human spaceflight history from 1981 to 2011.

Discovery was named after renowned sailing ships of exploration. It has
been preserved as intact as possible following its final flight in 2011.

---

Historical Significance

Space Shuttle Discovery represents a major period in the history of
human spaceflight and the U.S. Space Shuttle program.

Its 39 Earth-orbital missions, extensive time in space, and wide range
of mission types make it an important artifact for understanding the
development of reusable crewed spacecraft.

Discovery provides a useful example for studying:

- Human spaceflight
- Reusable spacecraft
- Space Shuttle technology
- Earth-orbital missions
- U.S. space exploration history
- Aerospace engineering

---

Transfer to the Smithsonian

NASA transferred Discovery to the Smithsonian in April 2012 following
a delivery flight over the nation's capital.

The spacecraft is preserved at the Smithsonian's National Air and Space
Museum.

ART008 — Bell X-1 "Glamorous Glennis"

1. Basic Information

- **Artifact ID:** ART008
- **Artifact Name:** Bell X-1
- **Alternate Name:** Bell X-1 "Glamorous Glennis"
- **Domain:** Space & Aerospace History
- **Subdomain:** Supersonic Flight / Experimental Aircraft
- **Date:** 1946
- **Manufacturer:** Bell Aircraft Corp.
- **Country of Origin:** United States of America
- **Type:** CRAFT-Aircraft

---

2. Historical Significance

The Bell X-1 was the first airplane to fly faster than the speed of sound.

On October 14, 1947, U.S. Air Force Captain Charles E. "Chuck" Yeager piloted the aircraft to a speed of approximately:

- **Speed:** 1,127 km/h (700 mph)
- **Speed:** Mach 1.06
- **Altitude:** 13,000 m (43,000 ft)

Yeager named the aircraft **"Glamorous Glennis"** in tribute to his wife.

The flight demonstrated that aircraft could be designed to fly faster than sound and helped establish practical supersonic flight.

---

3. Key Accomplishment

**Broke the Sound Barrier**

The X-1 proved that a manned aircraft could travel faster than the speed of sound and gathered important transonic flight data.

---

4. Development

The XS-1/X-1 program was developed through a cooperative program initiated in 1944 by:

- National Advisory Committee for Aeronautics (NACA)
- U.S. Army Air Forces

Bell Aircraft Corporation was contracted in 1945 to develop three transonic and supersonic research aircraft.

The aircraft was powered by a rocket engine and was air-launched from Boeing B-29 or B-50 Superfortress aircraft.

---

5. Aircraft Design

The Bell X-1 was a:

- Single-engine aircraft
- Single-seat aircraft
- Mid-wing rocket plane
- International-orange painted aircraft

Its smooth fuselage was based on the aerodynamic shape of a **.50-caliber machine-gun bullet**.

The fuselage contained:

- Two propellant tanks
- Twelve nitrogen spheres
- Pressurized cockpit
- Pressure regulators
- Retractable landing gear
- Wing carry-through structure
- Rocket engine
- Flight-test instrumentation

The aircraft used a **Reaction Motors, Inc. rocket engine** producing approximately **6,000 pounds of thrust**.

---

6. Flight History

The Bell X-1 completed a total of **78 flights**.

On March 26, 1948, Chuck Yeager reached:

- **Speed:** 1,540 km/h (957 mph)
- **Speed:** Mach 1.45
- **Altitude:** approximately 21,900 m (71,900 ft)

This represented the highest velocity and altitude reached by a manned airplane up to that time.

The X-1 continued flight-test operations until mid-1950.

It completed:

- 19 contractor demonstration flights
- 59 Air Force test flights

---

7. Impact and Innovation

The Bell X-1 demonstrated that the so-called **"sound barrier"** could be overcome by a manned aircraft.

Its flight-test program provided valuable transonic and supersonic flight data and contributed to the development of high-speed aircraft.

The X-1 therefore represents an important milestone in the transition from subsonic to supersonic aviation.

---

---

2. Historical Significance

The Mercury Pressure Suit was worn by astronaut **Alan B. Shepard Jr.** during the first manned spaceflight launched by the United States on **May 5, 1961**.

Shepard's sub-orbital flight was launched from **Pad 5 at Cape Canaveral** using a **Redstone rocket**. Approximately 15 minutes later, Shepard splashed down in the Atlantic Ocean.

The suit represents an important artifact from the early period of American human spaceflight and the **Project Mercury** program.

---

3. Suit Development

The Mercury spacesuit was a:

- Close-fitting suit
- Two-layer suit
- Full-pressure suit

It was developed by the **B.F. Goodrich Company** from their **Mark IV pressure suit**, which had previously been used by the U.S. Navy.

NASA selected the suit in **1959** for use during Project Mercury.

During the Mercury program, the suit underwent minor modifications, primarily involving the shoulders.

---

**Alan B. Shepard Jr.**

It also carries the iconic **Pioneer Plaque**, a gold-anodized aluminum plate featuring visual messages intended for potential extraterrestrial intelligence.

---

- **First Close-Up Exploration of Jupiter**
- **First Spacecraft on a Trajectory Out of the Solar System**

---

- **High-Gain Antenna:** 2.74-meter (9 ft) parabolic dish reflector
- **Power System:** Four Radioisotope Thermoelectric Generators (RTGs)
- **Scientific Instruments:** Magnetometer, Charged Particle Instrument, Cosmic Ray Telescope, Geiger Tube Telescope, Imaging Photopolarimeter
- **Interstellar Message:** Pioneer Plaque engraved with human figures, solar system map, and hydrogen hyperfine transition key.

Summary

This 3D model shows part of the skeleton of *Salwasiren qatarensis*, a 21-million-year-old species of fossil sea cow discovered in Qatar.

The fossils of *Salwasiren* were collected from the Al Maszhabiya bonebed, which is exposed throughout southwest Qatar, especially in a protected area called the Southern Reserve.

Its scientific name honors both the State of Qatar and the Bay of Salwa, a body of water close to where the fossils were found. The coastlines of the Bay of Salwa are shared by Saudi Arabia, Bahrain, and Qatar.

The bay supports herds of dugongs, the distant modern relatives of *Salwasiren*. Dugongs, like manatees from the Americas, are herbivorous marine mammals that eat plants on the seafloor.

*Salwasiren* weighed about as much as an adult panda or a heavyweight boxer, although its body size was relatively small compared to other fossil and living sea cows, including dugongs, which can weigh much more.

Today's dugongs use their tusks to excavate seagrass roots and create pits in the seafloor. This makes them ecosystem engineers because their activities support the health of seagrass ecosystems.

It is likely that *Salwasiren* occupied this ecological role in ancient seagrass ecosystems of the Early Miocene.

extended_knowledge.specimen_and_collector: Collected in 1891 by famed paleontologist John Bell Hatcher in the Lance Formation of Niobrara County, Wyoming (catalog USNM 4720).
extended_knowledge.historic_milestone: Mounted in 1905 at the Smithsonian, becoming the very first mounted Triceratops skeleton anywhere in the world and the world's most famous ceratopsian.
extended_knowledge.horns_and_frill: Features two massive 1-meter (3-foot) brow horns, a stout nasal horn, and a wide, solid bony neck frill (parietal-squamosal) that lacked the weight-reducing fenestrae (holes) of other ceratopsids.
extended_knowledge.defense_and_combat: Fossil bone frills and horns frequently exhibit healed puncture wounds and fractures, demonstrating active combat with rival Triceratops for territory and mates, as well as defense against Tyrannosaurus rex.
extended_knowledge.diet_and_size: Quadrupedal herbivore reaching 8 meters (26 feet) in length and 6 to 9 metric tons. Used a sharp keratinous parrot-like beak and shearing tooth batteries to slice fibrous palms, cycads, and ferns.

extended_knowledge.specimen_and_origin: Discovered in Late Pleistocene permafrost deposits of the Beringia region (Alaska and northern Siberia). Preserved with pristine microscopic dentin rings and enamel ridges.
extended_knowledge.tusk_adaptation: Spiraling ivory tusks reached up to 4.2 meters (14 feet) in length and over 80 kg in weight. Curved inward to prevent snagging in brush and used as snow shovels to sweep aside frozen snow drifts to reach grass.
extended_knowledge.molar_dentition: High-crowned (hypsodont) grinding molars composed of alternating vertical plates of hard enamel, dentin, and cementum. The plates acted as coarse rasps for grinding abrasive silica-rich tundra grasses and sedges.
extended_knowledge.cold_climate_adaptations: Equipped with dual-layer shaggy wool coats up to 90 cm long, 10 cm subcutaneous fat layers, small freeze-resistant ears and tail, and specialized cold-tolerant hemoglobin.
extended_knowledge.chronology_and_extinction: Abundant across the Holarctic steppe from 400,000 years ago until main continental extinction around 10,000 years ago, with isolated island populations surviving on Wrangel Island until 4,000 years ago.

extended_knowledge.tar_pits_preservation: Recovered from the asphalt seeps of the Rancho La Brea Tar Pits in Los Angeles, California. Petroleum permeated and petrified the bone, preserving pristine honey-brown fossilization.
extended_knowledge.saber_fangs: Iconic elongated maxillary canine teeth measured up to 28 cm (11 inches) long. Oval and serrated along both edges, designed to slice the windpipe and carotid arteries of heavy megafauna.
extended_knowledge.jaw_mechanics: Could open its jaws to an astonishing 120-degree gape angle (compared to 65 degrees for modern lions) enabled by modified mastoid processes and reduced lower jaw flanges.
extended_knowledge.hunting_style: Ambush predator with heavily muscled shoulders, neck, and forelimbs built to wrestle bison, horses, and juvenile mammoths to the ground before delivering a precision throat bite.
extended_knowledge.extinction: Disappeared approximately 10,000 to 11,000 years ago during the Quaternary extinction event following the collapse of large herbivore prey populations.
